title: Teaser Bets in Canada: When the Extra Points Pay Off
excerpt: Teaser bets buy points off the spread but cost you odds. Here is the maths behind teasers, the only spots worth taking, and where Canadians can bet them.
author: Jane Williams
bodyHtml:
With football season arriving, teaser bets return to the front page of every Canadian sportsbook app. The pitch is easy to like: take two or more sides, move each spread six points in your favour, and combine them into one wager. A three-point underdog becomes a nine-point underdog. A seven-point favourite only needs to win by two. It looks like the sportsbook is handing you a cushion. In reality a teaser bet in Canada is a parlay with a price attached to those points, and whether the trade is good or bad comes down to which numbers you are crossing.

How a teaser actually works

A standard teaser lets you adjust the point spread or total on every leg of a multi-leg bet by a fixed amount — six, six and a half, or seven points in football, four to five points in basketball. Every leg still has to win. If one loses, the whole ticket loses, exactly as with a parlay. In exchange for the extra points, the payout drops sharply. A two-team six-point football teaser typically pays around -120 to -130 rather than the +260 a straight two-team parlay would return.

That is the whole trade. You are not being given points; you are buying them, and the sportsbook sets the price. The question every serious bettor asks is whether the points you receive are worth more than the odds you surrender. Most of the time they are not. Occasionally they are very clearly worth more, and that gap is the only reason teasers are worth discussing at all.

Why key numbers decide everything

Football scores are not distributed smoothly. Because touchdowns are worth seven points with the conversion and field goals three, margins of victory cluster heavily on 3 and 7, with secondary clusters at 4, 6, 10 and 14. A margin of exactly three points is by a wide distance the most common outcome in professional football, and seven is second.

This is what makes some teaser legs valuable and others close to worthless. Moving a favourite from -8 to -2 crosses both 7 and 3 — the two most frequent margins in the sport. Moving an underdog from +1.5 to +7.5 does the same thing in reverse. Those six points are buying you a huge slice of probability. Moving a favourite from -12 to -6, by contrast, crosses 10 and 7, which is decent but noticeably weaker. Moving a spread from -19 to -13 crosses almost nothing that matters. The points are identical in every case; the value is not.

This is the reasoning behind the classic 'basic strategy' teaser that professional bettors have used for decades: tease favourites from between -7.5 and -8.5 down through the key numbers, and tease underdogs from between +1.5 and +2.5 up through them. Both moves cross 7 and 3. Everything else is a coin flip dressed up as a system.

The break-even maths

Understanding when a teaser is playable requires one number: your break-even win rate per leg. For a two-team six-point teaser priced at -120, the ticket needs to win about 54.5 per cent of the time overall. Because both legs must land, that translates to roughly 73.8 per cent per leg. At -130 you need closer to 76 per cent per leg.

That is a demanding bar. A straight bet at -110 only needs 52.4 per cent. Asking a single leg to win three times out of four is only realistic when the six points genuinely cross the fattest part of the scoring distribution — which is exactly why the key-number rule exists rather than being a stylistic preference. Historically, well-selected teaser legs of the type described above have cleared that threshold, though the edge is thin and shrinks whenever books shade their teaser pricing upward, which several have done as the play became widely known.

A few practical implications follow directly from the numbers:

  • Two-team teasers are the sweet spot. Adding a third leg compounds the requirement and rarely improves expected value unless every leg is a premium spot.
  • Price matters as much as the points. The same teaser at -110 and at -140 are completely different bets. Line shopping across books is not optional here.
  • Avoid totals in teasers. Game totals have no key numbers comparable to 3 and 7, so six points off a total is far less valuable than six points off a spread.
  • Ignore 'sweetheart' teasers. Ten-point teasers requiring three or four legs sound generous but are priced so heavily that the extra points never compensate.
  • Never tease a side you would not bet straight. Points do not fix a bad read on a game.

Where Canadians can bet teasers

Teasers are widely offered across the regulated Canadian market. Ontario's licensed books have supported them since launch, and they are standard on the Alberta platforms that came online in 2026. Availability varies more than the marketing suggests, though — some books cap teaser legs, restrict which sports qualify, or price two-team six-pointers noticeably worse than their competitors. If you intend to bet teasers at all, comparing that specific price across two or three accounts is worth more than any handicapping insight you will read this week. Our overviews of Ontario sports betting and Alberta sports betting cover which operators are live in each province, and the DraftKings sportsbook review looks at how one of the larger books handles multi-leg pricing.

If the terminology in this article is unfamiliar, the fundamentals are worth locking down first. Teasers are a derivative product built on top of point spreads, and they only make sense once spreads, juice and implied probability do — our primer on understanding the basics of sports betting is the right starting point.

The honest summary

Teasers are neither the free money the app suggests nor the sucker bet purists dismiss. They are a narrow, mathematical play that is profitable in a small number of clearly defined situations and mildly unprofitable everywhere else. The recreational bettor loses with teasers not because the product is rigged but because they use it as a comfort blanket — teasing whichever games they already fancied, at whatever numbers happen to be on the board.

If you cannot state which key numbers your six points are crossing, you are not making a teaser bet. You are making a parlay at bad odds and telling yourself it is safer. The players who make teasers work treat them as a tightly filtered weekly opportunity that some weeks simply does not appear — and when it does not, they pass.

You must be 19+ (18+ in some provinces) to gamble in Canada. If gambling stops being fun, free confidential help is available in every province.
